nodes.title: Terraform variables and locals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Terraform input variables make configurations reusable; locals simplify repeated expressions. The TF-003 exam heavily tests type constraints, validation blocks, sensitive flags, and the precedence order for variable assignment.

flashcards.front: Five ways to assign a Terraform variable (highest to lowest precedence)?
flashcards.back: -var flag > -var-file flag > *.auto.tfvars (alphabetical) > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR_name env var. Higher-precedence sources override lower ones.

flashcards.front: What does sensitive = true do on a variable?
flashcards.back: Redacts the value from CLI output and plan display. It does NOT encrypt the value in state — state still stores it in plaintext, so the backend must be secured separately.

flashcards.front: When to use locals vs variable?
flashcards.back: Use locals for computed or repeated expressions internal to a module that callers should not override (e.g. a concatenated name). Use variables for values callers should supply. Locals cannot be set from outside the module.

flashcards.front: Type constraint any vs object({ ... }) — trade-offs?
flashcards.back: object({ key = type }) enforces a specific schema with required keys and types — prefer this for safety. any disables type checking entirely and should only be used for dynamic wrapper modules where the type is intentionally unknown.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A user account 'jsmith' needs to be locked immediately without deleting the account or its data. Which command achieves this?
questions.explanation: usermod -L locks the account by prepending '!' to the password hash in /etc/shadow, preventing password-based login. userdel -r deletes the account and home directory. passwd -e forces the user to change their password at next login rather than locking the account. chage -I -1 sets the inactivity period but does not immediately lock the account.

questions.q: An administrator runs 'chage -l alice' and sees 'Password expires: Mar 01, 2026'. It is currently April. Alice can still log in with her password. What is the most likely reason?
choices: PAM is configured to ignore password expiry on this system
The account has INACTIVE days set to a high value allowing grace logins
The /etc/shadow file has a different expiry than chage reports
Alice's SSH key authentication bypasses password expiry checks
questions.explanation: The INACTIVE field in /etc/shadow defines a grace period in days after password expiry during which the user can still log in (but is forced to change the password). If INACTIVE is set to a large number, the user can continue logging in past the expiry date. PAM does enforce shadow expiry by default on standard configurations. chage reads directly from /etc/shadow so they match. SSH key authentication bypasses passwords entirely, but the question implies password login is working.

questions.q: After running 'useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel devuser', the administrator checks /etc/passwd and sees devuser's primary group is 'devuser', not 'wheel'. Why?
choices: The wheel group does not exist on this system so useradd fell back to the default group
The -G flag sets the primary group, which was overridden by useradd defaults
useradd creates a private primary group matching the username by default;.
The -m flag overrides group assignment and creates a new group
questions.explanation: By default, useradd creates a new primary group with the same name as the user (user private group scheme). The -G flag specifies supplementary groups, not the primary group. To set the primary group, you must use -g. So devuser's primary group is 'devuser' and 'wheel' is a supplementary group. If wheel didn't exist, useradd would error, not fall back silently. The -m flag only controls home directory creation. G adds supplementary groups

questions.q: A system is configured with UEFI firmware. During boot, the administrator needs to interrupt the GRUB2 menu to boot an older kernel. Which file contains the GRUB2 menu timeout setting?
questions.explanation: /etc/default/grub contains the GRUB_TIMEOUT and other configurable settings that are used as input by grub2-mkconfig to generate grub.cfg. The grub.cfg file is auto-generated and should not be edited directly. /etc/grub.d/40_custom is used for adding custom menu entries. grubenv stores boot environment variables like the saved default entry.

questions.q: A GRUB2 boot entry fails and the system drops to the GRUB rescue prompt. The administrator types 'ls' and sees '(hd0) (hd0,gpt1) (hd0,gpt2)'. Which sequence of commands boots the system?
questions.explanation: From the GRUB rescue prompt, you must set the root device, load the kernel with 'linux', load the initrd, then run 'boot'. The set root command points GRUB to the boot partition. grub-install and update-grub require a running OS. 'insmod normal; normal' is used from the GRUB shell (not rescue) to load the normal module if GRUB modules are available but GRUB's normal mode failed to load. initrd /initrd.img; boot

questions.q: A production system's GRUB2 boot menu shows two kernel entries. The older kernel is currently booting. An administrator wants to permanently set the newer kernel as the default. After updating /etc/default/grub with GRUB_DEFAULT=0, what must be run?
questions.explanation: After modifying /etc/default/grub, grub2-mkconfig regenerates the active grub.cfg from the templates in /etc/grub.d/ and the settings in /etc/default/grub. Without running this command, grub.cfg is unchanged and the setting has no effect. systemctl reboot just reboots without updating GRUB. grub2-install reinstalls the GRUB bootloader to the MBR/EFI partition, which is not needed here. update-grub is a Debian/Ubuntu wrapper equivalent to grub2-mkconfig but uses different output path syntax.

questions.q: A developer needs to give a script the ability to read files owned by root in /etc/ssl/private without giving the user root access. The script is at /opt/readcert.sh and is owned by root. Which permission configuration achieves this with least privilege?
choices: chmod 4755 /opt/readcert.sh to set the SUID bit so it runs as root
Add the developer to the root group and chmod 640 /etc/ssl/private
Set sticky bit on /etc/ssl/private with chmod +t
Create a dedicated group, add both root and the developer to it.
questions.explanation: Creating a dedicated group (e.g., sslreaders), adding the developer's user to it, changing the group ownership of /etc/ssl/private to sslreaders, and setting permissions to 640 or 750 provides access with least privilege. SUID on a shell script is ignored by Linux for security reasons. Adding the developer to the root group grants broad root-group access across the system, violating least privilege. The sticky bit on a directory only affects deletion, not read access. and chmod 640 /etc/ssl/private with group ownership

questions.q: An administrator needs to set a file permission of rwxr-x--- (owner: rwx, group: r-x, other: none) using chmod with numeric notation. Which command is correct?
questions.explanation: The permission rwxr-x--- breaks down as: owner (rwx = 4+2+1 = 7), group (r-x = 4+0+1 = 5), other (--- = 0). This gives 750. chmod 754 would set other to r-- (4), adding unwanted read access. chmod 755 sets other to r-x (5). chmod 740 sets group to r-- (4), removing execute from group.
